An Ancient Inheritance, Millions of
Years in the Making
Fossil fuels are formed from the remains of ancient plants and animals, buried deep inside
the Earth for millions of years. The immense heat and pressure from the Earth's crust
transformed this organic matter into concentrated energy sources.

sections.title: Page 3
sections.text:
The Coal Story: A World Drowned in
Green
The journey to create coal began over 300 million years ago. Earth was covered in
vast, dense swamp forests. As these giant plants and trees died, they sank to the
bottom of the swamps, creating thick layers of organic material.

sections.title: Page 4
sections.text:
From Living Forest to Buried Peat
Over time, these layers of dead plants were covered by soil, mud, and water.
This trapped the energy of the dead plants and, in the low-oxygen environment, they
partially decomposed into a dense, spongy, soil-like material called peat.
Burial & Compaction
Peat Formation
A) NotebookLM

sections.title: Page 5
sections.text:
The Alchemical Power of Heat and Pressure
As more and more layers piled on top, the weight of the ground, along with the Earth's
geothermal heat, created immense pressure. This process squeezed out water, hydrogen,
and oxygen, leaving behind a deposit rich in carbon—the substance we know as coal.
Intense Pressure

sections.title: Page 6
sections.text:
The Oil & Gas Story: Life in Ancient Seas
The origin of oil and natural gas is different, beginning in ancient oceans, lakes, and
rivers. Tiny marine organisms and plants, like plankton and algae, thrived in these
waters. When they died, they sank to the seafloor.

Unlocking the Buried Energy
To access these ancient energy stores, we must go deep into the Earth. Coal is extracted from
underground layers or 'seams' through extensive mining operations. Oil and natural gas are
reached by large drills that bore through rock to tap into the underground reservoirs.

The Engine of the Modern World
Fossil fuels are the primary engine of global civilization, providing the power for the Industrial
Revolution and our lives today. They are one of the most reliable and cheaper sources of energy.

Releasing a Million-Year Legacy in a Moment
The energy in fossil fuels is stored carbon. When we burn them for energy, we are releasing
that carbon, which had been locked away for millions of years, into the atmosphere in the
form of carbon dioxide (CO,).

A Legacy of Global Imbalance
This massive release of CO, is a potent greenhouse gas, which contributes to climate change and
global warming. The extraction and transport of these fuels also carry risks, from oil spills that
devastate marine ecosystems to the fact they are also a finite, non-renewable resource.

sections.title: Page 13
sections.text:
An Inheritance of Deep Time
It took hundreds of millions of years of Earth’s history to create our fossil fuel
reserves. We are consuming this ancient inheritance at a pace that is profoundly
faster than the natural processes that created it. The challenge is not just to find
new energy, but to respect the timescale of the energy we use.
